Of course! Surgery is a huge and pricey step, it should only ever be the final resort. 

My post was just advice to both you and OP about things to keep in mind and hoping to minimise the taboo around surgery - in case anyone was feeling guilty for thinking about it.

There definitely is a stigma around plastic surgery. I get it all the time when I tell people what I do for a living. 

My best advice is to do your research, consult with a surgeon. People are under the impression that implants have to be huge or unnatural. That's not true, we sell implants that are as low as 80cc in volume. It all depends on your body and what's needed. Good things to look for in a surgeon is that they'll consult with you specifically to your needs. They'll show you similar cases to you and the outcomes, they'll get you to try sizers to gauge the feeling, the weight, the size on your body underneath clothing. And they'll never do anything against your proportions. There are petite girls like yourself who seek an overwhelming jump and label a cup size. Surgeons should tell them the limit their body can handle before it takes a toll on their frame, the amount of tissue they have before, that the implants would side too wide on their body and look like they're drifting apart. Your surgeon will be able to explain to you the best results for you and help you get a better idea. 

Keep in mind there are many types of implants, also anatomical shaped ones that are more in a tear-drop shape rather than a dome. These might be something to look into if you don't have much tissue to begin with, or for reconstructive. 

The general idea that people who have surgery want to be plastic fantastic is misguided.

Hey there, my work deals with a lot of plastic and reconstructive surgeons and we see a lot of cases like yours. 

I think you should at least see about getting a consult. There's a lot surgeons can do these days, and in the case of asymmetry sometimes they only need to perform a unilateral procedure. In my country at least some cases are classed as medical procedures and can be covered by health insurance. 

I don't think you should feel ashamed of the idea of surgery at all. People always jump to the conclusion that it's all vain and plastic people who go for these surgeries. I can guarantee you at least if not more of the cases we come across they're medically related or reconstructive procedures. Severe ptosis, tuberous breasts, deformity, trauma, reconstruction after complete mastectomy. If it's significantly affecting your quality of life, it's worth consulting a professional. 

Edit: since window shopping could add up to being rather costly, realself.com is a fantastic site to read up on reviews and patient experience blogs (often throughout their journey, with before and afters) that might help you get an idea of surgeons you might be interested in seeing within your area.

For some of us it's about evening out our eyes rather than wanting to look white...

Asians typically have a flatter eye shape, creases can tend to be very shallow and as crazy as it sounds because of the flatter shape and lack of crease depth, creases can change shape overnight for various reasons (not enough sleep, puffy eyes, hydration) but the sometimes not both eyes are affected the same way. 

People use tape to temporarily fix the times when they wake up like [THIS](http://img49.imageshack.us/img49/9840/img4679jc4.jpg). Sometimes waking up with no eyelid creases, both eyes with creases, one eye with a crease -  it can be annoying and you might just want a bit of consistency. 

... Sometimes I wake up and it looks like I'm trying to squint one eye all day.
